Approach A: actual versus predicted daily demand

Frozen test, 28 February 2023 to 27 February 2024. Identical measured household support within each comparison.

364 scored days. No measurements exist for 29 October 2023, so that date remains a gap. Daily totals are in megawatt-hours (MWh).

Forecasting outcome

A reduced household errors, while portfolio improvement was modest. Daily-total mean absolute error was worse: 1.148 MWh versus 1.109 MWh for the lag benchmark.

Purchasing outcome

Under assumed 4:1 shortage-to-surplus penalties, A’s interval P80 purchases total 14.998 MWh. Historical simulated penalty fell 24.09% against buying A’s point forecast.

Final-day actual demand and actual tariffs are unavailable. Historical simulated penalty reduction does not establish final-day savings.

Inputs, missing data and model fitting

Two approaches to the same forecast task

28,180,608supplied meter rows
8weather stations
4homes without usable Total history
0targets actually reconstructed

A Weather and household context

  1. Validate the supplied data

    Parse timestamps and numeric readings, enforce unique household/time keys and check Total = HeatPump + Other. Retain measured zeros and extremes.

  2. Handle missing observations

    Leave missing targets unfilled. Reconstruct Total only when both components are valid; that filled zero rows here. Keep unknown inputs with missing indicators. Use a separate history-free model for four homes.

  3. Build features

    Forecast temperature, humidity and sunshine. Add available day/week lags, seven- and twenty-eight-day behaviour, calendar features, building and heating context.

  4. Fit and select the model

    Global histogram-based gradient boosting. Validation selects the configuration. Refit on eligible training and validation rows, then freeze model weights for the test.

80 boosting iterations · learning rate 0.07 · 15 leaves · minimum 200 samples per leaf · L2 regularization 2

B Recurring consumption patterns

  1. Clean observed records

    Drop invalid timestamps or targets, sort observations and retain the first duplicate. Reindex a regular UTC grid and leave gaps missing.

  2. Keep usable learning rows

    Exclude rows without all required lags and targets. Eligible homes need at least 1,344 complete training rows before calibration, 1,344 complete calibration rows and all 96 future day/week lag pairs.

  3. Fit a compact model

    Standardize inputs and fit global Ridge regression for each target date with penalty strength 1. Features are previous-day and previous-week demand plus sine/cosine representations of time and weekday.

  4. Calibrate and route fallbacks

    Reserve the preceding fourteen days for uncertainty calibration. Use week, day, historical-slot or portfolio profiles when Ridge eligibility fails.

Final routing: 372 Ridge · 11 prior-week · 23 historical profiles · 4 portfolio profiles

Data gaps, information cutoffs and modelling assumptions

The supplied rows contain 517,536 missing Total readings. Another 1,543,680 expected timestamps are absent within file bounds. These are separate counts. Seventeen households have no survey row.

A issues at 11:00 Europe/Berlin on the previous day, with assumed meter and weather arrival delays. B uses the complete preceding UTC day. Their information cutoffs differ. Undated survey information is assumed available throughout the benchmark.

Direct photovoltaic generation, electric-vehicle charging schedules and procurement prices are absent. The target is received Total electricity, interpreted as grid import. A uses missing indicators and unknown categories instead of treating missing demand as zero.

Sources: preprocessing report, locked A model configuration and supplied B source code. See Evidence for the exact files.

Metric definitions and the benchmark

MAE: mean absolute error, the average size of a prediction error. RMSE: root mean squared error, which gives larger errors more weight. WAPE: weighted absolute percentage error, the sum of absolute errors divided by the sum of measured energy.

A’s main benchmark is 75% previous-available matching local-slot demand plus 25% previous-week matching local-slot demand. This lag blend is separate from Approach B’s Ridge model.

Signed daily error = (forecast − actual) ÷ actual × 100. Positive means overprediction. Residual = forecast − actual at each interval. A near-correct daily total can still hide errors in the timing of demand.

Validation decisions and upstream forecast errors

Features, model choices and weather

Approach A: validation feature study

Portfolio weighted absolute percentage error. Lower values indicate smaller aggregate interval error.

Recent behaviour improved the chosen contextual model. Adding explicit photovoltaic ownership did not improve that configuration. Feature-group results are predictive comparisons, not causal estimates.

Selected configuration

105 columns, including missing indicators. Recent demand, predicted weather and building/heating context form the main model. Photovoltaic and electric-vehicle ownership remain inputs to the separate history-free model.

A serious benchmark

The lag blend reached 13.20% validation WAPE, better than A’s selected contextual model at 14.13%. On the annual test, their order reverses slightly.

Selected weather forecast: held-out mean absolute error

Weather procedure and additional modelling choices

Temperature and humidity use histogram-based gradient boosting. Sunshine uses the latest available matching hour, selected on validation. The demand model uses these forecasts rather than the future observed weather.

For demand, squared-error loss retained aggregate volume better than absolute-error loss, which underpredicted portfolio demand. Robust recent profiles, feature groups and extreme-reading sensitivity were assessed on validation. Large measured targets were retained.

The B description reports experiments with alternative trees and clustering without stable gains, but saved experiment outputs were not supplied for independent reproduction.

Approach A: 28 February daily quantities

What P10, P50 and P90 mean

P stands for percentile. P50 is the median of estimated demand. The P10–P90 range targets the middle 80% of modelled outcomes. The model point forecast is a separate estimate and need not equal P50.

How A estimated the range

A used validation prediction errors, scaled to forecast demand and conditioned on temperature where supported. Daily calibration uses complete daily error blocks. Four unobserved homes add provisional proxy uncertainty.

These are model-based estimates, not guaranteed probabilities. Test coverage applies to measured matched support, not verified ground truth for all 410 households. Individual interval coverage does not guarantee that every interval in a day is covered.

Conditional decision support

From a demand forecast to a purchase quantity

Actual tariffs were unavailable. All penalties below are assumed units per kWh.

28 February interval purchases

Why the cost ratio chooses this percentile

The cost ratio chooses the percentile. It balances the expected avoided shortage penalty against the expected added surplus penalty from a small extra purchase.

The validation errors determine the amount. For each forecast, A scales historical errors to that demand estimate and finds the selected percentile. It does not multiply the forecast by 80%.

Why 14.011 MWh and 14.998 MWh are different

14.011 MWh is the separately calibrated P80 for the whole-day net-demand objective. 14.998 MWh adds ninety-six interval P80 quantities, charging shortages and surpluses separately at each interval.

A daily percentile generally differs from a sum of interval percentiles. Different times can offset each other under net daily settlement. Their historical penalty reductions also differ: 26.22% daily and 24.09% interval for Approach A under 4:1.

The 14.998 MWh schedule total does not carry an 80% probability of covering the whole day. It sums marginal interval decisions.

“Optimal” here refers to expected linear imbalance penalty under the estimated demand distribution and assumed constant costs. Purchase prices, fees, market constraints and real execution were not modelled. No method or ratio was selected from test results. Final-day actuals are absent, so final-day savings are unknown.

Traceable numbers and practical limits

Evidence and interpretation

Supported outcomes

  • A improves annual household error against its validation-selected lag benchmark.
  • Both approaches produce a final forecast for all 410 homes.
  • A provides validation-calibrated demand quantiles and a fixed cost-ratio rule.
  • The same 4:1 interval rule lowers retrospective simulated penalty by 24.09% against A’s point-forecast purchasing.

Limits that affect the conclusion

  • B lacks an equivalent annual test and saved household predictions for common-support comparison.
  • Four homes lack measured Total demand history. Their forecast accuracy and uncertainty are unverified.
  • Daily coverage falls below the nominal target. Survey metadata has no historical effective dates.
  • There are no supplied actual prices or 28 February demand measurements.

Sources by result

Approach B historical provenance

The final report uses 294, 374 and 371 measured B homes on the three reported dates. The updated B description lists different complete-profile counts. The present B script only computes historical metrics when all 410 actual profiles exist. The published subsets cannot be reproduced independently from a supplied B prediction export.

Full forms and units

kWh
Kilowatt-hour, electricity energy.
MWh
Megawatt-hour, equal to 1,000 kWh.
UTC
Coordinated Universal Time. Each target day here has 96 intervals.
MAE
Mean absolute error.
RMSE
Root mean squared error.
WAPE
Weighted absolute percentage error.
P80
80th percentile of estimated demand. A quantity, rather than 80% of a forecast.
ML
Machine learning. In the procurement files it means Approach A.
PV / EV
Photovoltaic generation / electric vehicle.
